mortality.title: Mortality
mortality.subtitle: 7 days to make peace with the end

uncertainty.title: Living with Uncertainty
uncertainty.subtitle: 7 days to make peace with the unknown

people.title: Difficult People
people.subtitle: 7 days to stay calm with difficult people

mortality.title: Keep it in view
mortality.read:
You’re coming back from a funeral. No one in the car is talking. That evening everything looks a little different: the call you keep putting off, the sibling you’re not speaking to, the email that upset you yesterday. By morning the feeling is gone, and everything is back in its old place.

Epictetus told his students not to lose that feeling: keep death before your eyes every day; then you’ll never think a petty thought or want anything beyond measure.

This isn’t gloom. Thinking about death doesn’t darken life; it gives life back its proportions. The one who really puts things off is the one who never thinks about death, because they live as if they had endless time.

A frame doesn’t make the picture smaller; it shows you where to look.

Remembering that there is an end doesn’t take today away from you. It gives it back.

This program is for reflecting on death. If thoughts of death overwhelm you, or if you feel you don’t want to live, set the program aside and reach out to someone close to you or to a professional.
mortality.body: Stop once today and say to yourself: “I am mortal too.” Then go back to the first task of your day and notice what has changed.
mortality.ask: When you remembered you are mortal, what lost its importance, and what gained it?

mortality.title: Is it death that frightens you, or the thought of it?
mortality.read:
You woke up in the middle of the night. In the dark, the thought came: one day I won’t be here. Your chest tightened; you picked up your phone and looked at something else.

Epictetus says: it isn’t things that disturb people, but their judgments about things. Death isn’t terrible; if it were, it would have seemed terrible to Socrates too. Socrates spent his last day talking with his friends.

This isn’t “don’t be afraid”; fear doesn’t leave on command. What it says is: look inside the fear. Most of the time there isn’t one fear there, but several separate ones: suffering, leaving things unfinished, leaving the people you love, being forgotten. Each has its own answer, and for some of them there are things you can do today.

The shadow in the dark room, once you switch on the light, is a coat on a hook.

A fear you’ve named may not shrink. But now you can talk to it.
mortality.body: Write in one sentence what frightens you most about death: suffering, leaving things unfinished, the people you leave behind, being forgotten?
mortality.ask: Once you named the fear, did something come out of it that you can do today?

mortality.title: A little every day
mortality.read:
You’re looking at an old photo: you’re ten, it’s summer, your knees are covered in scrapes. Where is that child now? Not dead, but gone. That house, that voice, that summer won’t come back.

Seneca writes to his friend Lucilius: we’re wrong to think death lies somewhere ahead; most of it has already passed, and the years behind us are now in its hands. We don’t die all at once; we die a little every day.

It sounds bleak, yet it says the opposite: you’re no beginner at endings. Your childhood ended, school ended, maybe a city, a job, a love ended. You came through all of them, and you’re here.

In Seneca’s image: it isn’t the last drop that empties the water clock, but all the drops that ran before it.

The last day will be the last of something you already know.
mortality.body: Remember a chapter of your life you’ve left behind: childhood, a city, a job. Recall how you came through that ending.
mortality.ask: What did the end of that chapter teach you?

mortality.title: Alexander and his mule driver
mortality.read:
You’re at a wedding, or in a meeting. Who sits where, whose name gets mentioned first, is being discussed. You’re doing the math inside too: my title, my turn.

Marcus Aurelius, while he was the most powerful man of his age, wrote in his notebook: Alexander the Great and his mule driver, once dead, arrived at the same place.

This isn’t “nothing means anything.” The man who wrote it was back at work the next morning. What he’s saying is: fame and titles don’t pass through that door, so don’t spend yourself on them. The only thing left in your hands is what kind of person you are today.

When the game is over, the king and the pawn go into the same box.

Knowing this doesn’t make you smaller. It lifts a weight off your shoulders.
mortality.body: Ask something you’re chasing today: on the last day, will this still matter? If not, give part of the time you spend on it to something else.
mortality.ask: Which race did you step out of today, and what did that leave time for?

mortality.title: Settle the account every evening
mortality.read:
There’s someone you’ve been meaning to call “sometime”; it’s been months. A teacher you never thanked, a friend you never apologized to. They’re all waiting for “the right time.”

Seneca tells of an acquaintance’s sudden death: the man was planning business for years ahead, his ships, his profits; one evening he fell ill and didn’t live to see the morning. The lesson Seneca draws is this: let’s settle life’s account every day. Whoever puts the finishing touch on each day never runs short of time.

This doesn’t mean don’t make plans. Make long plans. But don’t tie the words that need saying to a plan.

A good shopkeeper counts the till in the evening before closing up. Not because they think they won’t open tomorrow; they sleep easy because they left their work in order.

Sleep at the end of a day whose account is settled is a different kind of sleep.
mortality.body: Finish one thing you’ve left half-done, today: a thank-you, an apology, a phone call.
mortality.ask: Which account did you settle today? When you did, what grew lighter inside you?

mortality.title: The ripe olive
mortality.read:
It’s autumn and you’re under a tree; the leaves are falling. No one calls this a disaster. But when we think of our own end, it feels as if there’s been some mistake, some injustice.

Marcus Aurelius reminds himself: don’t look down on death; it too is one of the things nature wills, just like growing, ripening, going grey. Spend this short time in keeping with nature and end your journey content: the way a ripe olive falls, praising the earth that bore it and thanking the tree that grew it.

This isn’t wanting death, or loving it. The olive is in no hurry to fall; as long as it stays on the branch, it ripens. Accepting isn’t giving up; it’s putting down the fight.

The olive that falls hasn’t lost. It has ripened.
mortality.body: Go outside and look at something the season is bringing to an end: a falling leaf, a fading flower, a shortening day. Don’t comment, just look.
mortality.ask: In the thing you looked at, what wasn’t sad?

mortality.title: Count what’s left as a gift
mortality.read:
A narrowly avoided accident, a test result that came back clear. For a few days everything looks like a gift: the smell of coffee, the sounds of the street, coming home. Then you get used to it.

Marcus Aurelius advises building that state on purpose: think of yourself as having died, accept that your life has been completed up to this moment; know that whatever comes after is extra, and live in keeping with nature.

This isn’t “live every day like it’s your last, wildly.” What changes isn’t the calendar but the way you look. You go to the same job, you sit at the same table; only with more attention.

A good guest doesn’t look for what’s missing at the table laid for them.

For seven days you’ve looked at the end. Now turn your head: ahead of you is a day given as extra.
mortality.body: When you wake up tomorrow morning, let your first thought be: this day was given as extra. Write down now what you’ll spend it on.
mortality.ask: Which moment today did you live as if it had been given as extra?

uncertainty.title: What are you waiting for?
uncertainty.read:
The test results come out on Thursday; today is Monday. You’re cooking, you’re talking to someone, but half your mind is always there.

Epictetus says: when I see someone anxious, I ask, what does this person want? If they didn’t want something outside their control, they wouldn’t be anxious. His example is a musician: playing alone, they’re at ease; on stage, their hand trembles. Because now they want not only to play well, but applause too.

This isn’t “want nothing”; wanting is human. But inside anxiety there is often a want that hasn’t been named, and a want without a name fills everything.

Knowing what you’re waiting for doesn’t make the wait shorter. But now you know what you’re sitting with.
uncertainty.body: Write in one sentence the uncertainty that has you waiting. Underneath, add: exactly which outcome do I want?
uncertainty.ask: When you wrote down the outcome you want, did your anxiety change: did it grow, or come into focus?

uncertainty.title: Suffering in imagination
uncertainty.read:
Your manager messaged in the evening: “Let’s talk tomorrow.” All night you were fired, you thought about the rent, you rehearsed how you’d tell your family. In the morning it turned out they wanted to ask about your holiday dates.

Seneca writes to his friend: there are more things that frighten us than things that crush us; we suffer more in imagination than in reality. Some things upset us more than they should, some before they should, and some when they shouldn’t upset us at all.

Seneca isn’t saying “bad things don’t happen”; they do. But if one happens, you suffer it once. Suffer it in advance, and you suffer it twice.

You’re paying interest on a loan you haven’t even taken out.

Most of the scenarios you build tonight won’t survive until morning. If one does, the you of the morning will meet it.
uncertainty.body: Count the bad scenarios that come to mind today; make a tally mark on a piece of paper. In the evening, look: how many actually happened?
uncertainty.ask: How many scenarios did you build, and how many came true?

uncertainty.title: The same chain
uncertainty.read:
You’re waiting for an answer to your application. You open your phone, refresh your email: maybe it’s come. A small hope, then a small drop. Fifty times a day.

Seneca passes on a saying of the philosopher Hecaton: stop hoping and you’ll stop fearing. Hope and fear look like opposites, but like a prisoner and the soldier guarding him, they’re bound to the same chain. Both send your mind off to a day that hasn’t come yet.

This isn’t telling you to be hopeless. You prefer the good outcome, you work for it. What you let go of is handing over today’s peace as a hostage to tomorrow’s news.

Let go of one end of the chain, and the other end loosens too.
uncertainty.body: Count how many times you check for the result today: phone, email, account. Then skip one check on purpose.
uncertainty.ask: How did that moment go when you didn’t check? Did you miss anything?

uncertainty.title: Take off the mask
uncertainty.read:
The question “What if it doesn’t work out?” goes round all day but never finishes. The sentence always breaks off in the same place; you don’t look at what comes after.

Seneca advises looking right there: whatever you fear, think of it as if it were going to happen, measure that evil and weigh your fear. You’ll see that it’s either not very big or not very long. Children are frightened even of people they know when they see them in masks; not only people, but things too, need their masks taken off.

This isn’t pessimism. The pessimist expects the worst and stays there. You look once, and plan the next morning.

A fear you’ve looked at all the way to the end takes up less room than one left half-seen.
uncertainty.body: Write down the worst outcome. Underneath, add three lines: what would I do the next morning?
uncertainty.ask: When you wrote down the worst, was it as big as it was in your imagination?

uncertainty.title: Not the ball, the game
uncertainty.read:
You’ve just come out of an interview. On the bus you replay every answer, as if you could change the result.

Epictetus points to people playing ball: none of them cares whether the ball is good or bad; they only care how to throw it and catch it. Socrates played like that in court, he says: the ball in play was his own life, and he played his game with skill.

This isn’t not caring about the result. A player wants to win. But whoever keeps their eyes on the scoreboard misses the ball coming at them.

Your job is the game. Wherever the ball lands, a game played well is yours.
uncertainty.body: On the thing you’re waiting for, make one move that’s in your hands today: a bit of preparation, a question, a message. Then let it go.
uncertainty.ask: What was your move today? After making it, could you let it go?

uncertainty.title: “If nothing stands in the way”
uncertainty.read:
Your holiday plan was perfect: tickets, hotel, weather forecast. In the morning a message came: flight cancelled. It felt as if the world had wronged you.

Seneca explains: the wise person begins everything with a reservation: “if nothing stands in the way.” That’s why nothing happens to them outside their expectations; they’ve counted from the start on the chance that something might come between.

This isn’t doing things half-heartedly. Make your plan fully, work fully. The reservation isn’t slackness; it’s flexibility.

A sailor charts the course but doesn’t bargain with the wind.

When your plan falls apart, what you’ve lost is the plan. You’re still standing.
uncertainty.body: Say one of today’s plans with this reservation: “I’ll do this, if nothing stands in the way.” Out loud or to yourself.
uncertainty.ask: Did something stand in the way today? If so, what did having the reservation change?

uncertainty.title: Only today’s load
uncertainty.read:
The result still hasn’t come. “How will I bear it if this goes on for months?” you think, and all those months land on your shoulders today.

Marcus Aurelius writes to himself: don’t overwhelm yourself by picturing your whole life at once. Don’t call up all the troubles that might come your way together; with each one, ask yourself: what is unbearable about this right now? Don’t let the future unsettle you; if you have to, you’ll reach it with the same reason you’re using today.

This doesn’t mean don’t think about the future; plans get made. But a load is only carried as much as today’s.

Look at every step of a staircase at once and you’ll tire. Your foot only ever lands on one.

For seven days you’ve been sitting with the unknown. It’s still unknown. But you’re no longer just someone who waits.

If anxiety has been disrupting your sleep, your work or your appetite for weeks, getting support from a professional is a Stoic choice too.
uncertainty.body: While the uncertainty goes on, choose one thing to live today fully, and do it: a walk, a meal shared, an unfinished task.
uncertainty.ask: Was there a moment today when you forgot what you’re waiting for? What were you doing in that moment?

people.title: Morning preparation
people.read:
Monday morning. Before you were even through the door you heard their voice, and your stomach tightened. You’ve known them for years, yet every time you’re surprised as if it were the first.

Marcus Aurelius would tell himself in the mornings: today I’ll meet meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsociable people. They act this way because they can’t tell good from bad. None of them can harm me, because no one can force me into anything shameful. Nor can I be angry with them; we were born to work together, like the hands and feet of one body.

This isn’t expecting the worst of people or turning cold on them in advance. It’s a preparation, so you won’t be surprised and won’t get angry.

Whoever knows it will rain takes an umbrella; they don’t sulk at the clouds.

What doesn’t surprise you tires you half as much.
people.body: Write the name of the difficult person on your mind. In the morning, tell yourself: “I may run into them today; I won’t be surprised.”
people.ask: Today, how did being prepared change that moment?

people.title: “It seemed so to them”
people.read:
Your colleague cut you off in the meeting again. The first sentence that goes through your head: they’re doing it on purpose.

Epictetus suggests a different sentence: when someone treats you badly or speaks badly of you, remember that they do it because they think it’s right. They follow their own view, not yours. If their view is wrong, they’re the one who is really deceived. Think this way and you’ll be gentle with whoever insults you, and each time you’ll say: “It seemed so to them.”

This isn’t proving them right. Understanding isn’t approving; wrong is still wrong. But the story “they’re doing it on purpose” only feeds your anger; the story “they’re seeing it wrong” leaves you options.

Whoever sets out with the wrong map gets lost; not to spite you.

You may not be able to fix their map. But now you know where they’re headed.
people.body: Write their latest behavior from their point of view, in one paragraph. Not to prove them right, but to understand.
people.ask: When you wrote it from their point of view, did what you saw surprise you?

people.title: Two handles
people.read:
You and your sibling argued over your mother’s care. Now when their name comes to mind, all that comes with it is the sentence they said that day.

Epictetus says: everything has two handles; take hold of one and it can be carried, take hold of the other and it can’t. If your brother wrongs you, don’t take hold of it by the handle “he wronged me”; it can’t be carried by that one. Take hold of it by the handle “he’s my brother, we grew up together.”

This isn’t ignoring the wrong; the wrong happened. But whichever handle you take, that’s what you carry. Take one and all you’re left holding is the wrong; take the other and you’re holding a relationship.

The second handle is always there. It just can’t be seen while you’re angry.
people.body: Find the handle between you and this person that can be carried, and write it down: what binds you? A shared past, a child, work in common, a kindness.
people.ask: When you took hold of the other handle, how did the same person look to you?

people.title: Look in the mirror
people.read:
The way they always talk about themselves drives you up the wall. In the evening you met a friend and spent an hour talking about them.

Marcus Aurelius advises: when someone’s fault bothers you, turn to yourself straight away and look at what similar fault you commit. When you see it, your anger soon dies down, because you understand that they too act this way under some pressure.

This isn’t “you’re the real culprit”; their fault is still a fault. The aim isn’t to beat yourself up, but to lower your finger.

When you point a finger, three point back at you.

Finding the same habit in yourself may not mean you’ve forgiven them. But you can no longer look down on them.
people.body: Write down the habit of theirs that angers you most. Then honestly look for a moment when the same habit showed up in you.
people.ask: What did you find in yourself? How did seeing it affect your anger?

people.title: Play your part
people.read:
Your father didn’t call again. On the holiday you called, on his birthday too. You ask yourself: is it always me?

Epictetus’s answer is harsh, but freeing: duties are measured by relationships. “But my father is a bad father.” Nature bound you not to a good father, but to a father. Don’t look at what he does; look at what you’ll do for your own share.

This isn’t saying yes to everything. Playing your own part doesn’t mean taking on his part too; you don’t have to make up for what he doesn’t do. Only your own share, in your own measure.

Even if the other actor forgets their line, a good actor doesn’t break their own role.

When you’ve done your share, the rest stops being your burden.
people.body: Today, do one thing that is your share in this relationship, and expect nothing in return.
people.ask: What did it feel like to do it without expecting anything back?

people.title: Teach or bear it
people.read:
Your neighbor makes noise until late every night. For months you’ve been grumbling under your breath and complaining to your partner; but you’ve never said a word to them.

Marcus Aurelius shows two paths in one short sentence: people exist for one another; so either teach them or bear with them. Elsewhere he adds: if you can, correct them by showing them; if you can’t, remember that patience was given to you for exactly this.

The order matters: teach first. Bearing it doesn’t mean swallowing it in silence, either. Stating your boundary in a calm voice is teaching itself. The third path, saying nothing and being angry, falls outside both.

A signpost doesn’t shout, but it doesn’t budge either.

When you say it, they may not change. But you’re no longer someone grumbling under your breath.

“Bear it” doesn’t apply to violence, threats or constant humiliation. If you’re in a relationship like that, your safety comes first; reach out to someone close to you or to a professional.
people.body: Write the one sentence you need to say to this person: without blame, calm, clear. Whether you say it is up to you.
people.ask: Did you write your sentence? Did you say it? If you didn’t, what held you back?

people.title: The best response
people.read:
They made a cutting remark. An even sharper one is on the tip of your tongue; if you say it, you’ll feel great for a moment.

In Marcus Aurelius’s notebook there’s a one-line note: the best revenge is not to become like them.

This isn’t backing down or swallowing it. You can answer, but in your own voice. A difficult person’s real power is making you like them: you shout at the one who shouts, sulk at the one who sulks, needle the one who needles.

When two people wrestle in the mud, both end up covered in it.

Seven days ago you wrote down a name. Maybe they haven’t changed at all. What has changed is who you are in front of them.
people.body: Notice the moment you want to respond the way they would, and answer in your own way.
people.ask: Which moment today were you able to respond without becoming like them?
